cards.explanation: The answer is “This is the camp of God.” Jacob sees the angels and says it, friends. (Genesis 32:2) Then he names the place Mahanaim. Angels walk up on the road and the man stops to name the spot. I'd have dropped my whole tray, mustache and all.

The word is servant, friends. Jacob tells his messengers to say, “Your servant Jacob says…” and to call Esau “my master.” (Genesis 32:4) I think Jacob is choosing his words very, very carefully. He's sending this message and he wants every word in its place.

The answer is True! Jacob says he sent the message “…so that I may find favor in your sight.” (Genesis 32:5) Look at the message itself, friends. He calls Esau “my master” and himself “your servant,” and then lists his oxen, donkeys, flocks, menservants and maidservants. I think that's a man walking up to a door with a full tray and a nervous smile.

The answer is four hundred men, friends. The messengers report that Esau is coming to meet Jacob, “…he and four hundred men with him.” (Genesis 32:6) That's a lot of company for a family visit. I'd be checking my pantry for extra cookies, and I'd still be nervous.

The answer is camps, friends. Jacob divides his people, the flocks, the herds and the camels into two camps. (Genesis 32:7) That's the first thing he does in his fear. I think a man who just heard "four hundred" wants to spread things out fast.

The answer is escape, friends. Jacob thinks, “If Esau comes and attacks one camp, then the other camp can escape.” (Genesis 32:8) I think a man who just heard about four hundred men coming wants a way out built into his plan (Genesis 32:6). Two camps means everything isn't sitting in one spot.

The answer is False. Jacob tells God, “I am unworthy of all the kindness and faithfulness You have shown Your servant.” (Genesis 32:10) He's not praying like a man with a list of reasons God owes him, friends. I think that's a humble way to pray with four hundred men on the road.

Jacob asks God to deliver him from Esau's hand, friends. He prays, “Please deliver me from the hand of my brother Esau…” (Genesis 32:11) He says it plainly and he says it to God. Sometimes that's the best prayer there is.
The answer is True, friends. Jacob says, “…I am afraid that he may come and attack me and the mothers and children with me.” (Genesis 32:11) He's not hiding his fear from God. He says it out loud.

The promise is offspring like the sand of the sea, friends. Jacob says, “But You have said, ‘I will surely make you prosper, and I will make your offspring like the sand of the sea, too numerous to count.’…” (Genesis 32:12) He brings God's own words right into his prayer. Next time you're at a beach, try counting the sand.

The answer is a gift, friends. Jacob spends the night there, and from what he had brought with him, he selects a gift for his brother Esau. (Genesis 32:13) He picks it out of his own animals, and the list starts with 200 female goats (Genesis 32:14). That's not a gift that fits in a bag.

Jacob tells his servants to keep some distance between the herds, friends! He entrusts the animals to them in separate herds and says, “Go on ahead of me, and keep some distance between the herds.” (Genesis 32:16) Picture it. Herd after herd, each one a little way behind the last, like a row of cookie sheets coming out one at a time instead of one big crowded tray. Jacob is sending gift after gift ahead of him.

The servant is to answer that the animals belong to Jacob, friends! Jacob tells the lead servant what to say if Esau asks: “They belong to your servant Jacob. They are a gift, sent to my lord Esau.” (Genesis 32:18) Then he adds, “And behold, Jacob is behind us.” So the servant doesn't just answer the question, he also tells Esau who's coming up the road. I think that's a message you'd rehearse a few times before you say it out loud.
The answer is True, friends. The servant is to say, “And behold, Jacob is behind us.” (Genesis 32:18) Esau hears about the gift and about Jacob in one breath. That's a lot to pack into a speech.

Jacob is hoping the gift will win Esau over before they meet, friends. He thinks, “I will appease Esau with the gift that is going before me. After that I can face him, and perhaps he will accept me.” (Genesis 32:20) The gift goes first and Jacob comes after. He's trying to soften Esau up before Esau sees his face.
The answer is False. Jacob thinks, “…perhaps he will accept me.” (Genesis 32:20) He's hoping, not sure, friends. Perhaps is a small word, but it's doing a lot of work in that sentence.
